situation:
You and your partner are the director of customer relations and the field operations manager at HELIOSTEAD SOLAR, a residential solar sales and installation company that serves one metropolitan area. The president (judge), the third generation of the founding family to lead the business, has asked the two of you to recommend how the company should finish this year's installation schedule.

HELIOSTEAD SOLAR began as a roofing company nearly sixty years ago and has sold and installed rooftop solar since the second generation took over. Almost all of its work still arrives by referral from a handful of older neighborhoods. BRIGHTBEND ENERGY, a national installer, opened a branch here in the spring, advertises lower prices, and has started calling homeowners who are already on the HELIOSTEAD SOLAR calendar.

The state rebate that pays for a large share of a residential system closes on December 31, and only systems inspected by that date qualify. HELIOSTEAD SOLAR sold forty-two installations against that deadline, and its two crews can finish about thirty. Every household moved past December 31 loses the rebate, and each of the forty-two has paid a deposit and holds an installation date in writing.

One of the forty-two agreements was signed by a seventeen-year-old who inherited a small house from a grandparent the founder served for decades. The teenager lives there with an aunt, who did not sign and has said she cannot take on the payments. Counsel advises that the teenager may cancel the agreement at any time, even after the panels are on the roof, leaving the company with an installed system it cannot collect on.

Dropping that installation would open a slot for a household whose agreement is enforceable and whose deposit is larger. The teenager says the rebate is the only reason the project is affordable, and the neighborhood that sends the company most of its referrals would watch a founder's customer's grandchild handed to BRIGHTBEND ENERGY. The president (judge) wants a recommendation on which installations stay on the calendar, what happens to the minor's agreement, and how the moved households will be told.

You will present your recommendation to the president (judge) in a meeting to take place in the president's office. The president (judge) will begin the meeting by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendation and have answered the president's questions, the president (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of HELIOSTEAD SOLAR, the third generation of the founding family to lead the company. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You have asked the director of customer relations and the field operations manager to recommend which of the forty-two sold installations stay on the calendar ahead of the rebate deadline, what the company should do about the agreement signed by the seventeen-year-old homeowner, and how the households that are moved past the deadline will be told.

You will listen to a schedule built on which agreements are enforceable and to a schedule built on which households the company has served longest, but in either case you want to hear what the company is giving up.

During the course of the presentation you are to ask the following questions of each participant team:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, how would we know we picked the right households?
If a customer we moved tells a neighbor we treated them unfairly, what would you want us to be able to point to?
